finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the caller-supplied token with PHP loose equality (==). An attacker who knows a victim's email can reset the victim's password without the real token. If $token comes from decoded JSON, sending boolean true makes true == 'any non-empty string' evaluate to true. If the stored token is a numeric-looking string such as '0e...', any other numeric-string token that evaluates to zero also matches through type juggling. The == comparison is also not constant-time.
finding.source: $email, $token and $new arguments of reset_password_loose, which are attacker-controlled request parameters. $token can be a non-string type such as JSON true or an array.
finding.sink: $db->exec UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at lines 5-6, which sets the victim's password.

trace.note: Fetches the stored token for the attacker-supplied email.
$row['token'] == $token uses loose comparison with attacker-typed input, so the check can be bypassed.
The password hash of the attacker-chosen $new is written to the account with that email.

finding.guards_checked: The SQL uses $db->quote(), so there is no SQL injection. The only authentication control is the token comparison, and it is loose. The sibling reset_password at line 14 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast and is safe. No type check on $token, no rate limiting, and no expiry or single-use invalidation of the token appears in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none (only SQL quoting via $db->quote, which doesn't protect the token check; no type check, no strict comparison)
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 uses `$row['token'] == $token` with no type check, so a JSON `true` token (or a '0e..' numeric-string collision) passes and reset.php:5-6 sets the victim's password; the function has no callers in this directory, so the caller's input typing is assumed from the finding's source claim.
